Sona stone throwing

By: Bernadette Maguire | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
The sequel to President Jacob Zuma’s State of the Nation Address unfolds over two afternoons from Tuesday as MPs take to the National Assembly podium to debate last week’s presidential remarks. With local government elections later this year, it’s the perfect opportunity to electioneer from all sides of the House - regardless of the cloak of parliamentary rules and protocol of this annual ritual in the national legislature.



Further information:
DA leader Mmusi Maimane already said he would table an economic growth plan for South Africa. The opposition party’s focus on the 8.3 million jobless South Africans was a feature, or at least a lapel button, at last Thursday’s SONA 2016. More can be expected on this point this week, alongside plans to combat drought, stimulate growth from a market-drive perspective and all that, in the wake of a post-SONA Twitter blitz: “8.3 million South Africans cannot find a job because President Zuma has one”.

Maimane as leader of the largest minority party in the national legislature – that’s the official parliamentary designation even though the DA prefers the title of leader of the opposition – is given the largest chunk of speaking time among those on the left side of the House (left, from the perspective of the presiding officer, that is). It remains to be seen if Maimane can live up to his “broken man” speech of last year, which is regarded by many as one of, if not the best speech in Parliament for a long time. It’s been a tough start to the year, as his DA became mired in its member Penny Sparrow’s description of black South Africans as “monkeys” – and the stage-managed anti-racism message delivered by Maimane at the Apartheid Museum last month has not quite captured the headlines as anticipated.

Economic Freedom Fighters' leader Julius Malema last year took to the podium to deliver a harsh repudiation of the ANC’s insistence it was delivering on the 1955 Freedom Charter in the year of the 60th anniversary of that milestone document. Given the new #ZuptaMustFall slogan (a reference to close links between Zuma and the Gupta families), there could be fireworks, particularly with the zero words the president spent on corruption in his speech last Thursday evening.

The EFF also has a point to prove, as the municipal poll in over 22,500 voting districts for the 257 or so councils will test its structures, established at break-neck speed following its 1.16 million vote performance in the May 2014 elections. Having promised to contest all wards, there’s much at stake: a lacklustre performance at the hustings may give the governing ANC sufficient ammunition to poo-poo the fighters; a good, or even excellent, performance will underscore the red brigade’s explosive entry onto the political landscape.

Given the EFF’s ability to adapt and fine-tune its political strategy and tactics to, in many ways, capture prevailing sentiments, the SONA 2016 debate is an opportunity not to be missed. Malema, as leader of the second biggest opposition party, will get the second largest slice of parliamentary speaking minutes, as determined by Parliament’s formula based on seats in the House. Malema has a track-record of using his minutes to the maximum.

The other 10 small opposition parties will battle with their speaking time, which is limited to three minutes for those with one MP like the Pan-Africanist Congress or ex-PAC MP turned leader of the African People’s Convention, Themba Godi.

But the focus this week must be on the ANC benches, and whom the governing party selects as its speakers in the parliamentary SONA 2016 debate. The ANC, of course, by virtue of its 249 seats in the House, gets the lion’s share of speaking time.

Who the ANC fields as speakers will be key. Will it be ministers and/or deputy ministers, who serve at the president’s pleasure in the Executive and can be expected to tow the correct line? Will it be committee chairpersons, who have a stake in continuing the correct line as their jobs could be on the line? Of course, the strategy may just be drawing into the laager in a show of unity, similar to the one seen immediately after last Thursday’s speech, when ANC MPs emerged from the National Assembly singing in favour of their president.

The news that Zuma’s lawyers at the Constitutional Court effectively had thrown the ANC parliamentary caucus under the bus emerged after the party’s two-day workshop by whips and committee chairpersons on the political strategy for the year ahead. It’s understood another meeting was called to discuss the implications of the legal arguments in ConsCourt.

The ANC in Parliament for two years vigorously defended the president by applying parliamentary rules and traditions in his favour as the Nkandla debacle dragged on. In an effort to close this particular bruising chapter in South Africa’s politics, the ANC MPs clung on to Police Minister Nkosinathi Nhleko’s report that even the non-security features like the R2.6 million swimming (fire) pool, cattle kraal, chicken run, visitors’ centre and amphitheatre were security features. That report, instituted by Zuma according to correspondence submitted to Parliament, was thrown out in legal arguments before the Constitutional Court last week, as the president conceded before the top judges of the land that the public protector’s findings on the presidential Nkandla homestead were not up for debate.

The governing party by no means is unified in its approach to the Nkandla debacle: in mid-2015 then ANC MP Paul Mashatile, now Gauteng ANC chairperson is back as MEC in his home province, distanced the party from the Nkandla spending at the Daily Maverick’s The Gathering. The ANC national executive committee (NEC), or highest decision-making structure between the elective conferences, had not taken a view on the matter, he said then. This Sunday’s newspapers reported on the rifts within the governing party: both City Press and the Sunday Times highlighted the party had advised Zuma to take the public protector’s report on review to court - the only legally-available option to challenge findings – or to simply make a plan to pay up.

Amid these dynamics it could be telling who takes to the podium for the governing ANC. What they will say is largely predictable, unless there is a radical shift away from previous years’ inputs. Traditionally, the ANC speakers use the presidential SONA address as a hook to showcase delivery of the governing party. Each speaker is allocated a topic – one speaks on state-owned enterprises, another on women, yet another on infrastructure etc etc - and underscores the ANC’s performance as “leader of society” amid repeated “Siyaquba! (We are moving forward)”. Of course, this being an election year, a good number of digs at the opposition are anticipated, and visa-versa.

The political grapevine has it the municipal poll would be held in early August. According to the law there is time until August 17, as the elections have to be held within three months of the date of the past election, or May 18, in the 2011 municipal poll.

All signs are that it will be a tricky two days’ of debating in the National Assembly. Zuma’s account of the state of the nation in 2016, while heavily focused on the economy, left much of the detail to Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan to flesh out in his Budget speech on February 24.

While cost cutting measures like limiting the numbers and size of overseas travel - Zuma may have taken a leaf out of the governance book of Tanzanian president John Magufuli, who limited his administration’s overseas flights shortly after taking office in November 2015 - may have been among the few concrete announcements, these are not new. Then called “cost containment measures”, or more colloquially the “haircut”, steps were already announced in December 2013. It’s understood departments pushed back, particularly around the limitations on ministerial cars. In his October 2015 medium-term budget policy statement (MTBPS), then finance minister Nhlanhla Nene said: “ We recognise that there is not yet full compliance with these measures”. Some DA number crunching (expect more of this this week) showed just R2 billion of were saved in the 2014/15 financial year from the previous year’s R25 billion spend on travel, entertainment, catering and use of consultants.

While Gordhan’s Budget speech no doubt is heavily anticipated in the current economic troubles, for now all that the MPs have is the president’s address. This week’s debate is the first of several opportunities to electioneer in the parliamentary calendar, including the budget vote debates that by law must be wrapped by mid-year and yet another DA motion of no confidence in the president.

It’s bound to be an interesting two afternoons - and on Thursday afternoon Zuma may just find his voice, lacking a week earlier in what has been described as a far from inspiring address on the state of the nation.

Press Release:


SONA Debate
The sequel to President Jacob Zuma’s State of the Nation Address unfolded this week as MPs took to the National Assembly podium to debate his speech. With the country on a precipice, opposition parties bombarded Zuma with insults and requests for him to wave the presidency goodbye. But will the 2016 SONA debate bring about change?


Script:


J STORY: SONA DEBATE
PRODUCER: BERNADETTE MAGUIRE
TX: SUNDAY 21FEBRUARY 2016
VISUAL VOICE

Inside Parliament
Eff leaving Defiant showdowns have characterized parliamentary debates over the past 2 years especially around the State of the Nation address with opposition parties finding their voices.

Upsound – Julius Malema
We want the date of when are you paying the money ..These things are the point of order .. the ones that you are hiding behind neh?


UP SOUND: JOHN LINK
Despite all the issues confronting our country including a potential downgrade to junk status for our economy, what was noticeable about the state of the nation debate was that it hardly focused on any of those issues – but rather on just one man, Jacob Zuma.

VO:14
Clad is his customary red overalls EFF leader Julius Malema was on form in a Tuesday tirade.

UP SOUND: JULIUS MALEMA
Mr Zupta, your legacy can be summed up in to three things: Umshin'wami. Nkandla. Guptas …And I am leaving. I can’t sit here to debate what you presented here because you are not a legitimate president. Bye bye!”
VO: 7
And DA leader Mmusi Maimane had tongues wagging with his star wars spoof speech.

UP SOUND: MMUSI MAIMANE
On Planet Zuma you can pretend the schools are working, that investors are lining up and State owned enterprises are thriving, but in the real world none of that is true.

MMUSI AT PODIUM He explained the metaphor in an interview this week.



UP SOUND: MMUSI MAIMANE
We have a president that is out of touch with the people of South Africa. He lives in this mythical world called Planet Zuma.


UP SOUND John
And when you talk about Planet Zuma – Do you think there are ANC MP’s who live there too? Or do they recognize that is not the reality?


UPSOUND: MMUSI MAIMANE
The most extraordinary thing that has happened to the ANC
… that here is the movement that used to be the defenders of freedom, now have become defenders of one man.



Exterior building
Naledi at podium VO:
Science and Technology Minister Naledi Pandor lashed back at the DA leader with an equally fanciful retort.


UP SOUND: NALEDI PANDOR
They live on a planet of their own making. Where their leader composes fairy tales full of monsters that are a figment of his imagination. In his fantasy world he is King of all he dreams .. and tries to use the fairytale as his “Lets pretend I will rule one day”.


VO: 11”
If the opposition overplay its hand they risk losing its stun effect – but this kind of robust debate is a sign of a healthy democracy says Professor Richard Calland.



UP SOUND: PROFESSOR Richard Calland
AUTHOR: THE ZUMA YEARS
Parliament has regained the public attention over the past year or so .. overall that has to be good for Democracy. You want Parliament to be the crucible for public discourse and the big debates of the day.


Zuma hand on heart VO: 4”
In stark contrast to Zuma’s State of the Nation address last week.





UP SOUND: PROFESSOR Richard Calland
AUTHOR: THE ZUMA YEARS
Well he arrived weakened and wounded. What we saw in the State of the Nation address was a man who was no longer really at the helm of government. The speech was not his. He barely had any sense of ownership over it. It was a speech that was written largely by Pravin Gordhan and by other officials in
treasury. And we now know who is running government again – it’s Treasury.


Zuma at podium VO:
Hardly surprising given the mounting scandals.


UP SOUND: PROFESSOR Richard Calland
AUTHOR: THE ZUMA YEARS
He’s a president whose reputation is in tatters.

Kodwa in office
VO:
But ANC Spokesman Zizi Kodwa says it’s a cheap trick to discredit the ruling party.

UP SOUND: Zizi Kodwa
ANC SPOKESPERSON
A sustained attack on the head of the ANC, is destroying the African National Congress. To discredit the head of the ANC, you discredit the entire organization.


TINYIKO AT LAPTOP.
CROWDS WITH EFF AND PRESS
VO:
Professor Tinyiko Maluleke warns that the opposition’s obsession could play into the President’s hands.


UP SOUND:
Tinyiko Maluleke
POLITICAL ANALYST UNIVERSITY OF PRETORIA.
They criticize him, they over reach, they over do it – he get’s sympathy from people and he survives.


VO; 7”
The ANC issued a statement this week registering its growing disgust with the shenanigans in the house.



UP SOUND: Zizi Kodwa
ANC SPOKESPERSON
It can’t Parliament - become a Boswell circus. Parliament have got rules, they can hackle, they can do everything , but youcan’t disrupt parliament.


JULIUS WITH ENTOURAGE OUTSIDE AT NIGHT VO 4”
Kodwa believes its nothing more than attention seeking behavior.


UP SOUND: Zizi Kodwa
ANC SPOKESPERSON
Firstly it’s a competition among opposition parties. Each of them, they are competing to be the main opposition party.
Secondly each of them they are chasing headlines.


VO: ..
ANC Stalwart and struggle veteran Mosiuoa Lekota who did prison time for the movement and now leads COPE vowed to continue challenging the president until he is held to account.


UP SOUND:
Mosiuoa “Terror” Lekota
COPE LEADER
I gave 13 and a half years of .. the best years of my life - I was in my youth, to get this constitution. I can no longer retreat from the compact we made. And to the end of my days I will continue to say, this is not what this constitution …that we fought for.


VO: 4”
And we can’t afford any more wrong turns he says.


UP SOUND:
Mosiuoa “Terror” Lekota
COPE LEADER
The country is very close to a cliff. If we don’t wake up timeously I’m afraid it may be too late.




VO: 8”
This week opposition parties put the President’s capitulation in the constitutional court under the spotlight.
Two years ago Jacob Zuma stood up in parliament and said this:

UP SOUND: Zuma – FROM 2014
“My residence in Nklanda has been paid for by the Zuma family.


UP SOUND: MMUSI MAIMANE
I was in Parliament when he made the statement to say
he has a bond to pay for his building in Nkandla. He is not willing to pay back any money because he built the property and that no one has made any determination.


Constitutional court VO:
Last week backed into a corner at the EFF driven Constitutional court bid just days before Sona, Zuma did an about turn when his lawyers conceded that he should abide by the Public Protectors decision to pay back some of the Nkandla money.



UP SOUND:
Mosiuoa “Terror” Lekota
COPE LEADER
I immediately realized he was lying to the house under oath.


VO: 7”
Lekota sees this as the ultimate breach of trust with the people the President is meant to serve.

UP SOUND:
Mosiuoa “Terror” Lekota
COPE LEADER
As things stand at the moment that office is occupied by an individual who is bound by no oath of office who does not deserve to be there.
UP SOUND: Zizi Kodwa
ANC SPOKESPERSON
Terror Lekota is a very angry man – he has become a recycled politician. Firstly when he was in the ANC, he has had many problems in the ANC. He’s got a personal vendetta with President Zuma.


VO: 7”
This week Lekota managed to stir up emotions in the house when his speech referenced factions in the legislature.


UP SOUND:
Mosiuoa “Terror” Lekota
COPE LEADER
Contrary to the anticipation of the authors of our constitution have been divided into two parts or factions.

VO: 3
It was taken on a point of order.
UP SOUND: RASERITI TAU
NCOP DEPUTY CHAIRPERSON
We don’t have factions in Parliament and therefore Honourable Member can you refrain from using words that are divisive in the house?

VO; 5
The DA’s Chief Whip John Steenhuisen leapt to his defense causing a fracas.

UP SOUND:
John Steenhuisen
DA Chief Whip
You are talking complete rubbish now and you are making this house a joke …. you are turning this house into a joke. You are not fit to sit in that chair … HONOURABLE MEMBER … how dare you, how dare you infringe on his right to freedom of speech.

VO: Steenhuisen was censured for using the word … rubbish.

UPSOUND: MMUSI MAIMANE
I think Parliament is the square at which political debate takes place and I think both those words, in my view, are entitled too – they are not unparliamentary.

VO: 4”
Cope’s Deidre Carter pointed out the speaker’s double standards.

UP SOUND:
Deidre Carter
Deputy General Secretary Cope :
Earlier today in the house we heard Minister Joemat-Petterson saying that members of the EFF were delinquent juveniles – no-one said a word. We talk about a faction, we are not attacking any individual. It is not a point of order.


Barbed wire going up Amid the heated exchanges the police took no chances when the President responded to the debate on Thursday.
Although the president didn’t address the scandals he did say all the right things.

UP SOUND: PRESIDENT JACOB Zuma:
The 2016 State of the Nation address is thus about uniting the country behind boosting economic growth, creating jobs and indeed to, a better life for all, our people.

VO: 11”
He also promised to clamp down on crime and corruption which in part saw the Rand rallying to R15,30 to the dollar. But is it a case of too little too late?


UP SOUND: JOHN WEBB LINK
The Parliamentary chamber this week echoed with calls for Jacob Zuma to step aside or be removed from office. But what isn’t clear is that if a change is to come, what it will be that brings it about?

VO: 4”
UDM leader Bantu Holomisa led the charge in parliament this week.
UP SOUND
GENERAL BANTU Holomisa
UDM LEADER
Place the interest and unity of the nation first. And vacate the office with dignity.
VO: 8”
Holomisa was unapologetic about his appeal saying the ANC and the opposition should work together on his exit strategy.

UP SOUND
GENERAL BANTU Holomisa
UDM LEADER
We are on a slippery slope unfortunately and it doesn’t seem to be any turnaround strategy ready to take us out of this quagmire.

UP SOUND:
Tinyiko Maluleke
POLITICAL ANALYST UNIVERSITY OF PRETORIA.
They almost jumped the gun because the Constitutional Court has reserved judgment. And all of them seem to based on what people think the Constitutional court will do or say. In that sense alone the calls sound a little too eager..


VO: 10”
This week it was announced that there will be a vote of no confidence in the President, on the 1st of March. But the opposition believes the answer lies at the Ballot box.

UPSOUND:
MMUSI MAIMANE
Believe you me if he loses more cities for the ANC they will be left with no choice.

Vo: Calland says we may see a shift in the National Executive Committee as well.
MINTASHI ???
UP SOUND:
Richard Calland
He has enjoyed the balance of power there for a long time. But my sense is things are changing. My view is that when MINTASHI smells change in the air and senses the ANC is turning against Zuma, He will turn too and he turns on a sixpence.

VO: 3”
If that happens it will have a domino effect.

UP SOUND:
Richard Calland
…There are key moments ahead: What will happen with Zma? What will happen with the ANC and the Municipal elections? How will the country handle tough economic times? for the next generation. Will it be able to continue to balance the budget? And who will the ANC elect to succeed Zuma – it will set the course for the next generation.







PROMOS ON NEXT PAGE




















Promo 1:

VO: 3
Tempers flared in the Sona debate this week.

John Steenhuizen:
This is rubbish…not fit to sit on that chair

VO: 3
We ask is the robust debate healthy?


Promo 2:

VO: 5”
President Jacob Zuma’s fitness to hold office took centre stage at the Sona debate.

Julius:
You are not fit to be president…bye bye.

VO: 4
We ask is it all just hot air or is number 1 in trouble?

Promo 3

VO:
It was a week filled with new planets, angry outbursts, hurled insults and stone throwing at the Sona debate. Electioneering? Or do the opposition parties have a point?

UP SOUND: Mosiuoa “Terror” Lekota COPE LEADER Contrary to the anticipation of the authors of our constitution have been divided into two parts or factions. VO: 3 It was taken on a point of order. VO: 11” He also promised to clamp down on crime and corruption which in part saw the Rand rallying to R15,30 to the dollar. But is it a case of too little too late? But what isn’t clear is that if a change is to come, what it will be that brings it about? VO: 4” UDM leader Bantu Holomisa led the charge in parliament this week. UP SOUND GENERAL BANTU Holomisa UDM LEADER Place the interest and unity of the nation first. And vacate the office with dignity. UP SOUND GENERAL BANTU Holomisa UDM LEADER We are on a slippery slope unfortunately and it doesn’t seem to be any turnaround strategy ready to take us out of this quagmire. UP SOUND: Tinyiko Maluleke POLITICAL ANALYST UNIVERSITY OF PRETORIA. They almost jumped the gun because the Constitutional Court has reserved judgment. VO: 10” This week it was announced that there will be a vote of no confidence in the President, on the 1st of March. But the opposition believes the answer lies at the Ballot box. UPSOUND: MMUSI MAIMANE Believe you me if he loses more cities for the ANC they will be left with no choice. Vo: Calland says we may see a shift in the National Executive Committee as well. MINTASHI ??? UP SOUND: Richard Calland He has enjoyed the balance of power there for a long time. But my sense is things are changing. My view is that when MINTASHI smells change in the air and senses the ANC is turning against Zuma, He will turn too and he turns on a sixpence. VO: 3” If that happens it will have a domino effect. UP SOUND: Richard Calland …There are key moments ahead: What will happen with Zma? What will happen with the ANC and the Municipal elections? How will the country handle tough economic times? for the next generation. Will it be able to continue to balance the budget? And who will the ANC elect to succeed Zuma – it will set the course for the next generation. PROMOS ON NEXT PAGE Promo 1: VO: 3 Tempers flared in the Sona debate this week. John Steenhuizen: This is rubbish…not fit to sit on that chair VO: 3 We ask is the robust debate healthy? Promo 2: VO: 5” President Jacob Zuma’s fitness to hold office took centre stage at the Sona debate. Julius: You are not fit to be president…bye bye. VO: 4 We ask is it all just hot air or is number 1 in trouble? Promo 3 VO: It was a week filled with new planets, angry outbursts, hurled insults and stone throwing at the Sona debate. Electioneering? Or do the opposition parties have a point?

metadata.Summary: The sequel to President Jacob Zuma’s State of the Nation Address unfolds over two afternoons from Tuesday as MPs take to the National Assembly podium to debate last week’s presidential remarks. With local government elections later this year, it’s the perfect opportunity to electioneer from all sides of the House - regardless of the cloak of parliamentary rules and protocol of this annual ritual in the national legislature.
metadata.Further information: DA leader Mmusi Maimane already said he would table an economic growth plan for South Africa. The opposition party’s focus on the 8.3 million jobless South Africans was a feature, or at least a lapel button, at last Thursday’s SONA 2016. More can be expected on this point this week, alongside plans to combat drought, stimulate growth from a market-drive perspective and all that, in the wake of a post-SONA Twitter blitz: “8.3 million South Africans cannot find a job because President Zuma has one”. Maimane as leader of the largest minority party in the national legislature – that’s the official parliamentary designation even though the DA prefers the title of leader of the opposition – is given the largest chunk of speaking time among those on the left side of the House (left, from the perspective of the presiding officer, that is). It remains to be seen if Maimane can live up to his “broken man” speech of last year, which is regarded by many as one of, if not the best speech in Parliament for a long time. It’s been a tough start to the year, as his DA became mired in its member Penny Sparrow’s description of black South Africans as “monkeys” – and the stage-managed anti-racism message delivered by Maimane at the Apartheid Museum last month has not quite captured the headlines as anticipated. Economic Freedom Fighters' leader Julius Malema last year took to the podium to deliver a harsh repudiation of the ANC’s insistence it was delivering on the 1955 Freedom Charter in the year of the 60th anniversary of that milestone document. Given the new #ZuptaMustFall slogan (a reference to close links between Zuma and the Gupta families), there could be fireworks, particularly with the zero words the president spent on corruption in his speech last Thursday evening. The EFF also has a point to prove, as the municipal poll in over 22,500 voting districts for the 257 or so councils will test its structures, established at break-neck speed following its 1.16 million vote performance in the May 2014 elections. Having promised to contest all wards, there’s much at stake: a lacklustre performance at the hustings may give the governing ANC sufficient ammunition to poo-poo the fighters; a good, or even excellent, performance will underscore the red brigade’s explosive entry onto the political landscape. Given the EFF’s ability to adapt and fine-tune its political strategy and tactics to, in many ways, capture prevailing sentiments, the SONA 2016 debate is an opportunity not to be missed. Malema, as leader of the second biggest opposition party, will get the second largest slice of parliamentary speaking minutes, as determined by Parliament’s formula based on seats in the House. Malema has a track-record of using his minutes to the maximum. The other 10 small opposition parties will battle with their speaking time, which is limited to three minutes for those with one MP like the Pan-Africanist Congress or ex-PAC MP turned leader of the African People’s Convention, Themba Godi. But the focus this week must be on the ANC benches, and whom the governing party selects as its speakers in the parliamentary SONA 2016 debate. The ANC, of course, by virtue of its 249 seats in the House, gets the lion’s share of speaking time. Who the ANC fields as speakers will be key. Will it be ministers and/or deputy ministers, who serve at the president’s pleasure in the Executive and can be expected to tow the correct line? Will it be committee chairpersons, who have a stake in continuing the correct line as their jobs could be on the line? Of course, the strategy may just be drawing into the laager in a show of unity, similar to the one seen immediately after last Thursday’s speech, when ANC MPs emerged from the National Assembly singing in favour of their president. The news that Zuma’s lawyers at the Constitutional Court effectively had thrown the ANC parliamentary caucus under the bus emerged after the party’s two-day workshop by whips and committee chairpersons on the political strategy for the year ahead. It’s understood another meeting was called to discuss the implications of the legal arguments in ConsCourt. The ANC in Parliament for two years vigorously defended the president by applying parliamentary rules and traditions in his favour as the Nkandla debacle dragged on. In an effort to close this particular bruising chapter in South Africa’s politics, the ANC MPs clung on to Police Minister Nkosinathi Nhleko’s report that even the non-security features like the R2.6 million swimming (fire) pool, cattle kraal, chicken run, visitors’ centre and amphitheatre were security features. That report, instituted by Zuma according to correspondence submitted to Parliament, was thrown out in legal arguments before the Constitutional Court last week, as the president conceded before the top judges of the land that the public protector’s findings on the presidential Nkandla homestead were not up for debate. The governing party by no means is unified in its approach to the Nkandla debacle: in mid-2015 then ANC MP Paul Mashatile, now Gauteng ANC chairperson is back as MEC in his home province, distanced the party from the Nkandla spending at the Daily Maverick’s The Gathering. The ANC national executive committee (NEC), or highest decision-making structure between the elective conferences, had not taken a view on the matter, he said then. This Sunday’s newspapers reported on the rifts within the governing party: both City Press and the Sunday Times highlighted the party had advised Zuma to take the public protector’s report on review to court - the only legally-available option to challenge findings – or to simply make a plan to pay up. Amid these dynamics it could be telling who takes to the podium for the governing ANC. What they will say is largely predictable, unless there is a radical shift away from previous years’ inputs. Traditionally, the ANC speakers use the presidential SONA address as a hook to showcase delivery of the governing party. Each speaker is allocated a topic – one speaks on state-owned enterprises, another on women, yet another on infrastructure etc etc - and underscores the ANC’s performance as “leader of society” amid repeated “Siyaquba! (We are moving forward)”. Of course, this being an election year, a good number of digs at the opposition are anticipated, and visa-versa. The political grapevine has it the municipal poll would be held in early August. According to the law there is time until August 17, as the elections have to be held within three months of the date of the past election, or May 18, in the 2011 municipal poll. All signs are that it will be a tricky two days’ of debating in the National Assembly. Zuma’s account of the state of the nation in 2016, while heavily focused on the economy, left much of the detail to Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan to flesh out in his Budget speech on February 24. While cost cutting measures like limiting the numbers and size of overseas travel - Zuma may have taken a leaf out of the governance book of Tanzanian president John Magufuli, who limited his administration’s overseas flights shortly after taking office in November 2015 - may have been among the few concrete announcements, these are not new. Then called “cost containment measures”, or more colloquially the “haircut”, steps were already announced in December 2013. It’s understood departments pushed back, particularly around the limitations on ministerial cars. In his October 2015 medium-term budget policy statement (MTBPS), then finance minister Nhlanhla Nene said: “ We recognise that there is not yet full compliance with these measures”. Some DA number crunching (expect more of this this week) showed just R2 billion of were saved in the 2014/15 financial year from the previous year’s R25 billion spend on travel, entertainment, catering and use of consultants. While Gordhan’s Budget speech no doubt is heavily anticipated in the current economic troubles, for now all that the MPs have is the president’s address. This week’s debate is the first of several opportunities to electioneer in the parliamentary calendar, including the budget vote debates that by law must be wrapped by mid-year and yet another DA motion of no confidence in the president. It’s bound to be an interesting two afternoons - and on Thursday afternoon Zuma may just find his voice, lacking a week earlier in what has been described as a far from inspiring address on the state of the nation.
